caption: A composite grid of twenty panels from Josef Albers' 'Homage to the Square' series. Each panel features a standardized geometric composition of three or four nested squares. The series explores the 'interaction of color,' demonstrating how the perception of a single hue changes based on its proximity to others. Albers used these consistent forms to investigate optical effects like simultaneous contrast and spatial depth, where colors may appear to recede or advance. The grid showcases a wide spectrum of color relationships, from monochromatic harmonies to vibrant, clashing contrasts.

A small white dog sleeps on the floor, and various domestic items like a cupboard and a side table populate the room, grounding the occult act in a familiar setting.

caption: An 18th-century Polish devotional engraving serving as a frontispiece or illustration for a religious text titled 'DRELOWANIE CZWARTE' concerning the Blessed Sacrament of the Altar. The central focus is a monstrance containing the Host placed on an altar covered with a cloth inscribed 'Wszystkim Wszystko' (All to everyone). Above the altar are three emblematic cartouches: on the left, a pillar representing constancy; in the center, the 'Pelican in her Piety' feeding her young with her own blood, a classic symbol of Christ's sacrifice and the Eucharist; and on the right, a burning candle symbolizing self-sacrifice for others. Flanking the altar are an angel with a trumpet on the left and a female personification, likely Faith or Charity, on the right holding a plate of bread. The base of the image features an oval vignette depicting a ship at sea with a saintly figure on deck, labeled 'Z daleka' (From afar), representing the Church navigating the world (Navis Ecclesiae).

caption: The painting depicts the Adoration of the Magi, a biblical scene from the Gospel of Matthew. The Virgin Mary is seated, holding the Christ Child who reaches out to the kneeling elderly Magus, traditionally identified as Melchior, who has removed his crown in an act of humility and adoration. To the left, a bearded Magus, often identified as Caspar, stands holding a richly ornamented golden chalice or ciborium, representing frankincense or gold. To the right, an African Magus, traditionally Balthasar, stands holding a golden orb, likely symbolizing gold, and a feathered cap. caption:
The Scene
At the top centre, a radiant burst of divine light (the Holy Spirit) descends, sending tongues of flame onto the gathered figures — small red flickers visible above several heads.

The interior is a Flemish domestic space — tiled chequered floor, a large fireplace, leaded windows

caption:
This is Saint Veronica with the Sudarium, painted around 1500 by the Master of the Legend of Saint Ursula — an as yet unidentified late 15th-century Flemish master who was one of the most important masters working in Bruges in the late 15th century and a contemporary of Hans Memling. 
Veronica, with her exotic headgear and flapping headscarves, has veiled her eyes and looks down at the cloth she holds. It is said to portray the true face of Christ — the Vera Icon — which is in fact the origin of Veronica's name.
The panel has an arched top, with the saint set against a gilt background. Her elaborate clothing and headdress are bejeweled, and the veils on either side of her head are animated as if in the wind. Christ is shown looking straight ahead at the viewer, depicted in exacting detail. 
The elongated bodies and egg-shaped heads are typical of the Ursula Master's style, clearly visible here.

See: https://www.museabrugge.be/en/news/nieuwe-aanwinst-voor-musea-brugge

The library ceiling fresco cycle was painted by the Milanese artist Pellegrino Tibaldi (1527–1596), based on a humanist program devised by the library's first librarian. The vault is divided into seven zones representing the seven liberal arts — the Trivium (Grammar, Rhetoric, and Dialectic) and the Quadrivium (Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Astrology). Each discipline is personified by an allegorical figure. In this panel, Astrology is depicted as a regal woman seated among clouds, surrounded by putti and figures holding astronomical instruments such as an armillary sphere. The word ASTROLOGIA is inscribed on a banner below her. 

For Tibaldi see also: https://www.getty.edu/vow/ULANFullDisplay?find=Pellegrino+Tibaldi&role=&nation=&prev_page=1&subjectid=500124327

caption:
Castello della Manta: Fountain of Youth

Authorship & Date
The work is attributed to the anonymous "Master of Castello della Manta" and was completed soon after 1420. It was commissioned by Valerano of Saluzzo, the illegitimate son of the Marchese Tommaso III, between 1411 and 1416. 

Subject & Iconography
On the southern wall of the Sala Baronale, the myth of eternal youth is depicted by the fountain of youth, surmounted by the god of Love. 
The central Gothic fountain dominates the composition, topped by a small figure of Cupid (the god of Love). Around it, a lively crowd of figures in rich Late Gothic dress approaches from both sides — nobles, monks, elderly men and women — all eager to bathe and be restored to youth.
In the fresco, travelers are shedding their clothes and stripping off their stockings. On the side, some figures are climbing into the water. Inside the basin, rejuvenated couples are engaged in playful interactions. 

The lush green trees, the richly colored garments (reds, blues, yellows, whites), and the animated crowd give the scene a festive, almost theatrical energy — a rare and vivid window into 15th-century courtly imagination.

caption: The central engraving shows an allegorical female figure standing on a decorated column/pedestal inside a classical arched interior with columns on either side. caption:
This is a richly illuminated manuscript page depicting Christ as Salvator Mundi ("Savior of the World"), a common iconographic type in late medieval and Renaissance art, likely from a Book of Hours or similar devotional manuscript.
Central image:
Christ is shown half-length, facing forward, with long brown hair and a forked beard
He wears a rose/pink robe (possibly a chemise or tunic) with a bejeweled clasp at the neck featuring a large cross-shaped brooch with colored gemstones
His right hand is raised in a gesture of benediction (blessing), with two fingers extended
His left hand holds a globe/orb (representing the world) topped with a cross — the defining attribute of the Salvator Mundi type
A radiant gold halo with cruciform rays surrounds his head, set against a deep blue background
The blue field is filled with fine gold radiating lines suggesting divine light or glory

Lower register:
A smaller framed scene beneath shows a narrative episode, appears to depict a Way to Calvary / Road to Golgotha scene — figures with ladders, tools, and a group of soldiers or workers, possibly preparing the cross or engaged in the Passion narrative

Left border:
An ornate architectural frame in gold with grotesque/candelabra-style ornament (scrollwork, vase-like elements)
Two small grisaille (monochrome) figures stand in niches within the border, likely representing prophets or saints, rendered in a statue-like grayscale technique typical of Flemish/Netherlandish manuscript illumination

caption: An engraved illustration from a 17th or 18th-century Polish devotional book, specifically focusing on the 'Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar.' The central composition features a monstrance displaying the Eucharist placed on an altar-like chest decorated with symbols. Above the altar are three emblematic medallions: a column representing stability, a pelican in her piety symbolizing Christ's sacrifice, and a burning candle symbolizing the light of Christ. To the left stands an angel with a trumpet, and to the right is a veiled female figure, likely an allegory of Faith or the Church, holding a vessel. At the bottom, a medallion depicts a ship sailing on the sea, a traditional symbol for the Church (Navis Ecclesiae) navigating towards salvation. The Polish text provides a theological reflection on the spiritual food provided by the Eucharist.

A small, chubby child leans intimately toward the man's face, with a piece of white drapery around their waist. The background features a dramatic, cloudy sky. The painting is presented in a dark frame with an inscription at the bottom attributing the work to Nicolas van Heilst (1614–1669).
